docs.title: Servebench
docs.text: Load-test any OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint with statistical rigor, hardware telemetry, and automated bottleneck diagnosis.

docs.title: Why Servebench?
docs.text:
Benchmarking LLM serving engines (vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, SGLang, LM Studio, TGI) is notoriously difficult: - Client Conflation: Many benchmark tools schedule requests on busy client event loops, reporting artificial client-side scheduling latency as slow server response time. - Statistical Inaccuracy: Tools frequently report "p99 latency" on 10 or 20 requests—a mathematical fallacy where p99 is simply the sample maximum. - Conflated Timings: Standard TTFT mixes client network transit, server FIFO queue delays, and prompt evaluation compute into a single opaque number. - Black-box Servers: Benchmarks typically observe only external HTTP response streams, ignoring internal GPU power draw, VRAM usage, and server queue depth.

Servebench solves these problems: 1. Accurate Timings & Client Lag Monitoring: Continuously monitors client event loop lag and flags runs where the client is the bottleneck. 2. Statistical Rigor: Enforces sample count awareness (\(N \ge 100\) for honest p99s), multi-trial repeats with Student's t 95% confidence intervals, and steady-state throughput calculations. 3. P11 Server Breakdown: Isolates queueing overhead from prompt evaluation: Queue Overhead = Client TTFT - Server Prefill. 4. GPU Telemetry (NVML): Measures real-time GPU power (W), temperature, clocks, and computes energy efficiency in Tokens per Joule. 5. Automated Bottleneck Diagnosis: Automatically identifies if the system is Slot/Queue-Bound, Memory-Bandwidth-Bound, Compute-Bound, or Client-Bound. 6. CI Performance Regression Gate: servebench check candidate.json --baseline base.json to block deployments that regress latency or throughput. 7. Hardware Roofline Model (servebench roofline): Computes Memory Bandwidth Utilization (MBU %) and Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU %) with ASCII curves. 8. Automated Parameter Optimizer (servebench tune): Detects throughput saturation knees and generates production launch configurations. 9. Interactive Serving Monitor (servebench top): Real-time TUI streaming GPU power, VRAM, Tokens/Joule, and queue metrics.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install via pip or uv: 

pip install servebench
Or with optional dependencies (e.g. for mock server): 
pip install "servebench[mock]"

docs.title: 1. Instant Local Benchmark (servebench quick)
docs.text:
Auto-detects any running local server (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio) on standard ports and runs a 1-minute capacity test: 

servebench quick

Output: 

servebench quick: Ollama 0.6.0 at http://127.0.0.1:11434, model qwen2.5:0.5b
  c=1   16 ok, 0 failed,  64.2 tok/s, TTFT p50 43 ms
  c=2   16 ok, 0 failed, 126.8 tok/s, TTFT p50 44 ms
  c=4   16 ok, 0 failed, 203.1 tok/s, TTFT p50 47 ms
  c=8   16 ok, 0 failed, 241.5 tok/s, TTFT p50 115 ms

Ollama 0.6.0, qwen2.5:0.5b on Intel Core i7-13700H, NVIDIA RTX 3050 6GB (driver 551.76)
  Capacity: 4 concurrent users at once (203 tokens/s, first token in 47 ms)
  At 8 users: first token slowed to 115 ms (server queues requests for available slots)

docs.title: 2. Full Concurrency Sweep (servebench run)
docs.text: servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 --model llama-3-8b --concurrency 1,2,4,8,16 --repeat 3

docs.title: 3. CI Regression Gate (servebench check)
docs.text:
Fail your CI build if TTFT p50 increases by \(>15\%\) or throughput drops by \(>10\%\): 

servebench check candidate.json --baseline baseline.json

docs.title: 4. Hardware Roofline (servebench roofline)
docs.text:
Analyze MBU % and MFU % against theoretical limits: 

servebench roofline results/ollama-np4.json --gpu-name "RTX 3050 Laptop"

docs.title: 5. Automated Server Tuning (servebench tune)
docs.text:
Derive optimal concurrency limits and copy-pasteable launch flags: 

servebench tune results/ollama-np4.json --engine ollama

docs.title: 6. Real-Time Monitor (servebench top)
docs.text:
Live GPU telemetry and serving throughput monitor: 

servebench top --inline

docs.title: CI/CD Performance Regression Gating Guide
docs.text: Learn how to integrate Servebench into your CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) to catch latency degradations and throughput regressions before deploying model updates to production.

docs.title: 1. Why Gate Serving Performance in CI?
docs.text:
When updating: - Engine versions (e.g. vLLM or llama.cpp upgrades) - Model quantization configurations (e.g. FP16 to FP8 / AWQ) - Serving hyperparameters (--max-num-seqs, chunked prefill, prefix caching)

A regression in TTFT or token throughput can silently degrade end-user response times or spike GPU cloud infrastructure costs. servebench check acts as an automated quality gate that returns exit code 1 if regressions exceed acceptable tolerances.

docs.title: 2. GitHub Actions Integration
docs.text:
Create .github/workflows/servebench-regression.yml:

name: Serving Performance Regression Gate

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  performance-gate:
    runs-on: self-hosted # or GPU runner with access to LLM server
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install Servebench
        run: |
          pip install servebench

      - name: Benchmark Candidate Server
        run: |
          servebench run \
            --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 \
            --model target-model \
            --concurrency 1,4,8 \
            --num-requests 50 \
            --out candidate_run.json

      - name: Download Baseline Run
        run: |
          # Download established baseline from S3, release artifact, or git LFS
          curl -sSL https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/baselines/target-model-baseline.json -o baseline_run.json

      - name: Evaluate Regression Tolerances
        run: |
          servebench check candidate_run.json \
            --baseline baseline_run.json \
            --max-ttft-degradation-pct 15.0 \
            --max-tpot-degradation-pct 10.0 \
            --max-throughput-degradation-pct 10.0 \
            --max-error-rate-pct 1.0

      - name: Upload Candidate Run Artifact
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: benchmark-results
          path: candidate_run.json

docs.title: 3. Exit Codes & Gating Logic
docs.text:
• Exit Code 0: All tested load levels satisfied regression limits. The pull request passes.
  • Exit Code 1: One or more metrics degraded beyond configured limits (e.g., TTFT increased by \(>15\%\), throughput dropped by \(>10\%\), or error rate exceeded \(1\%\)). The CI pipeline blocks merge.

docs.title: CLI Command Reference
docs.text: This document provides a complete reference for all Servebench CLI commands and options.

docs.title: 1. servebench quick
docs.text:
Automatically probes local ports (11434 for Ollama, 8080 for llama.cpp, 8000 for vLLM, 1234 for LM Studio) to identify running engines, tests model capacity for ~1 minute, and prints clear human-readable serving capacity.

servebench quick [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• --url TEXT: Explicit server URL (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1).
  • --model TEXT: Model identifier to benchmark. If omitted, queries the server's /models endpoint and selects the active model.
  • --max-users INT: Upper limit of concurrent users to test (default: 32).
  • --api-key TEXT: Authorization bearer token if required by server.
  • --out PATH: Destination path for results JSON (default: servebench-quick-<engine>-<model>.json).

docs.title: 2. servebench run
docs.text:
The primary load-testing command. Executes closed-loop concurrency sweeps or open-loop Poisson arrival rate benchmarks with full control over input/output distributions, repeats, GPU telemetry, and Prometheus metrics.

servebench run [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Essential Options
docs.text:
• --url TEXT: Server API base URL (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1).
  • --model TEXT: Model name.
  • --concurrency TEXT: Comma-separated list of concurrent in-flight streams (e.g. 1,2,4,8,16).
  • --rate TEXT: Comma-separated list of Poisson request arrival rates in req/s (e.g. 5,10,20). Pass inf for all-at-once burst.
  • --repeat INT / -r: Number of independent repeat trials per load level (default: 1). Computes mean ± spread and Student's t 95% confidence intervals.
  • --config PATH / -c: Path to YAML, TOML, or JSON benchmark configuration file.

docs.title: Workload & Traffic Shaping
docs.text:
• --preset [chat|rag|code|agent]: Standard workload preset for input/output token lengths:
  • chat: 128 input / 256 output tokens.
  • rag: 2048 input / 128 output tokens.
  • code: 512 input / 512 output tokens.
  • agent: 1024 input / 384 output tokens.
  • --input-len INT: Average prompt length in tokens (default: 256).
  • --output-len INT: Target generation length in tokens (default: 128).
  • --input-dist [fixed|normal|lognormal|uniform]: Input token length distribution.
  • --output-dist [fixed|normal|lognormal|uniform]: Output token length distribution.
  • --burstiness FLOAT: Gamma shape parameter \(k\) for request arrivals (default: 1.0 = Poisson; \(<1.0\) = burst clusters followed by pauses).
  • --shared-prefix-tokens INT: Common token prefix shared across requests to benchmark server KV cache reuse.
  • --trace PATH: Path to a JSONL file with recorded user queries to replay.

docs.title: Observability & Telemetry
docs.text:
• --gpu-telemetry / --no-gpu-telemetry: Collect GPU core utilization, VRAM usage, and power draw via pure-Python NVML (default: enabled).
  • --scrape-metrics [auto|URL]: Scrape Prometheus /metrics exposition format before and after each level.

docs.title: Export & Reports
docs.text:
• --out PATH: Path to save run.json.
  • --csv PATH: Path to export level summary statistics as CSV.
  • --csv-requests PATH: Path to export raw per-request timing traces as CSV.

docs.title: 3. servebench check
docs.text:
CI Performance Regression Gate. Compares a candidate benchmark run against a baseline run and exits with code 1 if regressions exceed thresholds.

servebench check CANDIDATE_JSON --baseline BASELINE_JSON [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Regression Thresholds
docs.text:
• --max-ttft-degradation-pct FLOAT: Maximum allowed TTFT p50 latency increase percentage (default: 15.0%).
  • --max-tpot-degradation-pct FLOAT: Maximum allowed TPOT p50 latency increase percentage (default: 10.0%).
  • --max-throughput-degradation-pct FLOAT: Maximum allowed throughput drop percentage (default: 10.0%).
  • --max-goodput-degradation-pct FLOAT: Maximum allowed goodput drop percentage (default: 10.0%).
  • --max-error-rate-pct FLOAT: Maximum allowed request failure percentage (default: 1.0%).

docs.title: 4. servebench compare-models
docs.text:
Renders a side-by-side terminal comparison table across multiple benchmarked models or engine configurations.

servebench compare-models run1.json run2.json [run3.json ...]

Compares: - Peak Output Throughput (tok/s) and relative delta (+/-%) - TTFT p50 (ms) - TPOT p50 (ms) - Goodput (tok/s meeting SLO) - Average Power Draw (W) - Energy Efficiency (Tokens per Joule) - Primary Bottleneck Diagnosis

docs.title: 5. servebench find-context-limit
docs.text:
Systematically tests increasing prompt context lengths (doubling from start to max) to determine the maximum workable context window before GPU out-of-memory (OOM) or request timeout.

servebench find-context-limit --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 --model llama-3-8b --start 512 --max 32768

docs.title: 6. servebench find-capacity
docs.text:
Automates doubling search and binary search to identify the exact saturation knee where latency crosses target SLOs.

servebench find-capacity --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 --model llama-3-8b --slo-ttft-ms 500 --slo-tpot-ms 50

docs.title: 7. servebench report
docs.text:
Generates terminal tables, interactive HTML reports with charts, and CSV files from one or more saved run.json files.

servebench report run.json --out report.html

docs.title: 8. servebench share
docs.text:
Generates ready-to-copy Markdown tables and social share preview cards (1200x630 PNG) to include in GitHub issues or blog posts.

servebench share run.json

docs.title: 9. servebench mock-server
docs.text:
Runs an out-of-process OpenAI-compatible mock server with deterministic microsecond timings. Used for testing, calibration, and CI verification.

servebench mock-server --port 8000 --ttft-ms 100 --itl-ms 20

docs.title: 10. servebench top
docs.text:
Real-time interactive terminal UI dashboard displaying live GPU telemetry, Prometheus server metrics, queue depth, and dynamic throughput/TTFT sparklines.

servebench top [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• --url TEXT / -u: Server API base URL (default: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1).
  • --refresh FLOAT / -r: Dashboard refresh interval in seconds (default: 0.5).
  • --duration FLOAT / -d: Exit after N seconds (useful for scripts/testing).
  • --inline: Render inline directly in the terminal scrollback without switching to alternate screen buffer.

docs.title: 11. servebench roofline
docs.text:
Evaluates LLM serving performance against theoretical hardware limits using the Roofline model. Computes Memory Bandwidth Utilization (MBU %), Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU %), arithmetic intensity, and renders an ASCII roofline chart.

servebench roofline [OPTIONS] [RUN_FILE]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• RUN_FILE: Optional path to a run.json benchmark file.
  • --model TEXT / -m: Model identifier (e.g. qwen2.5:0.5b, llama3:8b-q4_k_m).
  • --gpu TEXT / --gpu-name / -g: GPU device name override (e.g., rtx 3050, a100, t4).
  • --bandwidth FLOAT / --gpu-mem-bw / -b: Manual memory bandwidth override in GB/s.
  • --peak-tflops FLOAT / --gpu-tflops: Manual peak FP16/BF16 compute override in TFLOPs.

docs.title: 12. servebench tune
docs.text:
Analyzes concurrency sweeps to identify throughput saturation knees and latency SLO boundaries, outputting recommended engine launch flags and environment variables.

servebench tune [OPTIONS] [RUN_FILE]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• RUN_FILE: Optional completed run.json to derive recommendations from. If omitted, runs an automated sweep against --url.
  • --engine TEXT / -e: Target engine override (ollama, vllm, llamacpp, mini-infer).
  • --target-ttft-ms FLOAT: Target TTFT p50 latency threshold in ms (default: 150.0).
  • --target-itl-ms FLOAT: Target ITL p50 latency threshold in ms (default: 40.0).
  • --url TEXT / -u: Base URL of OpenAI-compatible server (default: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1).
  • --model TEXT / -m: Model name when running automated sweep (default: qwen2.5:0.5b).

docs.title: Serving Engine Configuration & Tuning Guide
docs.text: Servebench automatically identifies and benchmarks all major LLM serving engines through standard OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoints. This guide details optimal configurations, internal timing support, and Prometheus metrics for each engine.

docs.title: 1. Engine Compatibility Matrix
docs.text: Engine Auto-Detect Port Fingerprint API Server Timing Breakdown (P11) Prometheus /metrics Recommended Flags for Benchmark Ollama 11434 /api/version ✓ (prompt_eval_duration) - OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4 llama.cpp 8080 /props ✓ (timings.prompt_ms) ✓ (/metrics) --parallel 4 -fa --cont-batching vLLM 8000 /version Via Prometheus ✓ (/metrics) --max-num-seqs 64 --enable-prefix-caching mini-infer 8000 /health (engine: mini-infer) ✓ - mini-infer serve --port 8000 SGLang 30000 /get_model_info Via Prometheus ✓ (/metrics) --mem-fraction-static 0.85 LM Studio 1234 /api/v0/models - - Enable local server in Developer tab

docs.title: Ollama
docs.text:
• Default Concurrency Bottleneck: By default, Ollama configures single-stream execution. To test multi-user batching, set: 
    export OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4
export OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1
ollama serve
  • Localhost IPv6 Quirk on Windows: On Windows, connecting to http://localhost:11434 may attempt IPv6 ::1 before falling back to IPv4 127.0.0.1, injecting ~300 ms of connection delay into TTFT. Always use http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1.

docs.title: llama.cpp Server (llama-server)
docs.text:
• Enabling Server Metrics: Run llama-server with --metrics to expose Prometheus metrics at /metrics: 
    llama-server -m model.gguf -c 4096 --parallel 4 -fa --cont-batching --metrics
  • Streaming Timings: llama.cpp natively returns timings: {prompt_ms, predicted_ms} in the final stream chunk. Servebench extracts this automatically to isolate server prefill vs decode durations.

docs.title: vLLM
docs.text:
• Prometheus Scraper: vLLM exposes /metrics by default on its serving port. Use --scrape-metrics auto in Servebench to track:
  • vllm:num_requests_waiting: Pending FIFO queues.
  • vllm:num_requests_running: Active batched slots.
  • vllm:gpu_cache_usage_factor: KV cache VRAM pressure.
  • vllm:prefix_cache_hit_rate: Prefix caching effectiveness.

docs.title: SGLang
docs.text: • RadixAttention & Prefix Reuse: Benchmark SGLang's RadixAttention using Servebench's --shared-prefix-tokens 512 flag to observe TTFT reduction from KV cache reuse.

docs.title: mini-infer
docs.text:
• Zero-Dependency Continuous Serving: Pure Python/PyTorch inference engine featuring Paged KV-Cache, chunked prefill, and speculative decoding.
  • Auto-Detection: Servebench recognizes mini-infer via its /health status and parses /v1/chat/completions usage chunks.
  • Launch Command: 
    mini-infer serve --port 8000

docs.title: Learn LLM Inference by Measuring It
docs.text:
A hands-on guide to how LLM inference systems work under the hood.

Instead of reading abstract math or architecture diagrams, you will run 7 reproducible experiments on your own machine using servebench and Ollama. Every experiment explains the systems concept, gives the exact command to run, and shows the real numbers measured on a laptop GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3050 6 GB Laptop GPU with qwen2.5:0.5b).

All raw benchmark data for these experiments is committed in results/learn/ and results/.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Install servebench: 
    pip install servebench
  2. Install and start Ollama with a small model: 
    ollama run qwen2.5:0.5b ""
  3. Verify connection: 
    servebench quick

docs.title: Experiment 1: The Prefill Phase (TTFT vs. Prompt Length)
The Concept
docs.text:
An LLM request has two fundamentally different phases: 1. Prefill (Prompt Processing): The server ingests the entire prompt in one parallel forward pass. It calculates Key and Value projections for all prompt tokens and populates the KV Cache. Because all tokens are known simultaneously, prefill saturates the GPU's compute cores (tensor cores). 2. Time to First Token (TTFT) measures how long the user waits before the first word of the response appears. TTFT is dominated by: $\(\text{TTFT} \approx \text{Prefill Time} + \text{Queue Wait} + \text{Network / HTTP Overhead}\)$

If prefill processes tokens in parallel, how does TTFT scale as prompt length grows?

docs.title: The Experiment
docs.text:
Send 8 single requests (\(c=1\)) with fixed generation length (64 tokens) while scaling input prompt length from 16 to 2,048 tokens:

# 16 prompt tokens
servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 --model qwen2.5:0.5b \
    --concurrency 1 --num-requests 8 --input-len 16 --output-len 64 --out results/learn/prompt-16.json

# 256 prompt tokens
servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 --model qwen2.5:0.5b \
    --concurrency 1 --num-requests 8 --input-len 256 --output-len 64 --out results/learn/prompt-256.json

# 1024 prompt tokens
servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 --model qwen2.5:0.5b \
    --concurrency 1 --num-requests 8 --input-len 1024 --output-len 64 --out results/learn/prompt-1024.json

# 2048 prompt tokens
servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 --model qwen2.5:0.5b \
    --concurrency 1 --num-requests 8 --input-len 2048 --output-len 64 --out results/learn/prompt-2048.json

docs.title: Real Measured Numbers (RTX 3050 6 GB)
docs.text:
(Source: results/learn/prompt-*.json)

Prompt Length TTFT p50 TTFT p99 Prefill Speed 16 tokens 22.6 ms 24.1 ms baseline overhead 256 tokens 42.2 ms 45.0 ms ~12,800 tok/s prefill 1,024 tokens 116.1 ms 122.4 ms ~10,500 tok/s prefill 2,048 tokens 215.5 ms 224.8 ms ~10,500 tok/s prefill

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
• Linear prefill scaling: Above the ~20 ms baseline (network, HTTP parsing, model dispatch), TTFT scales linearly with prompt length at approximately ~95–100 ms per 1,000 prompt tokens on this GPU.
  • Why this matters for system design: When designing RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) or chat agents, adding a 2,000-token retrieved context imposes an unavoidable ~200 ms latency tax on TTFT before generation even starts.

docs.title: Experiment 2: The Decode Phase (TPOT is Constant)
The Concept
docs.text:
Once the first token is generated, the model switches to the Decode Phase: * Autoregressive generation produces exactly one token at a time. * To generate a single token, the GPU must fetch every single model weight from VRAM into registers/cache, perform matrix-vector multiplication with the latest token, read the past KV cache, and output logits. * Time Per Output Token (TPOT) (or Inter-Token Latency, ITL) measures the gap between streamed tokens. * Because the arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte loaded) of processing one token is tiny (\(\sim 1\)), the decode phase is strictly memory-bandwidth bound, not compute-bound!

Does generating tokens become slower if the input prompt was 2,048 tokens instead of 16 tokens?

docs.title: The Experiment
docs.text: Inspect the TPOT recorded in the same four runs from Experiment 1:

docs.title: Real Measured Numbers (RTX 3050 6 GB)
docs.text: Prompt Length Output Tokens TPOT p50 Output Throughput 16 tokens 64 4.91 ms / token 203.8 tok/s 256 tokens 64 4.92 ms / token 203.3 tok/s 1,024 tokens 64 5.03 ms / token 198.7 tok/s 2,048 tokens 64 5.13 ms / token 194.8 tok/s

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
• TPOT is nearly invariant to prompt length: Across a 128× increase in prompt length (16 → 2048 tokens), TPOT barely shifted (4.91 ms vs 5.13 ms, a 4% difference caused by reading the larger KV cache).
  • The Arithmetic Proof:
  • Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4_K_M occupies \(\sim 0.63\text{ GB}\) in VRAM.
  • RTX 3050 Laptop GPU memory bandwidth: \(\sim 168\text{ GB/s}\) theoretical (\(\sim 125\text{ GB/s}\) realistic).
  • Time to read 0.63 GB model weights once: $\(\frac{0.63\text{ GB}}{125\text{ GB/s}} \approx 0.00504\text{ seconds} = 5.04\text{ ms}\)$
  • Our measured TPOT of 4.91 ms matches the hardware bandwidth limit almost perfectly!

docs.title: The Concept
docs.text:
If single-stream decode is memory-bandwidth bound, how do servers serve hundreds of users? * If 4 requests generate tokens simultaneously, the GPU loads the model weights from VRAM once and multiplies them against 4 tokens simultaneously. * This amortizes memory bandwidth across multiple streams, dramatically boosting overall throughput (out tok/s). * In Ollama, concurrency capacity is determined by OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL (execution slots).

What happens when we run with 1 slot vs. 4 slots vs. 8 slots?

docs.title: The Experiment
docs.text:
Run a concurrency sweep (\(c=1, 2, 4, 8\)) with 64 requests per level, varying OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL:

# Terminal 1: Start Ollama with 4 parallel slots
OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4 ollama serve

# Terminal 2: Run sweep
servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 --model qwen2.5:0.5b \
    --concurrency 1,2,4,8 --input-len 256 --output-len 128 --out results/ollama-np4.json

docs.title: Real Measured Numbers (RTX 3050 6 GB)
docs.text:
(Source: results/ollama-parallel.md)

Slots (NUM_PARALLEL) Concurrency (\(c\)) Total Throughput Single-Stream TPOT TTFT p50 1 slot \(c=1\) 190 tok/s 4.9 ms 45 ms 1 slot \(c=4\) 199 tok/s (no gain!) 4.8 ms 1,840 ms (queued!) 4 slots \(c=4\) 385 tok/s (2.0× boost) 9.4 ms 101 ms 8 slots \(c=8\) 400 tok/s (plateau) 16.0 ms 224 ms

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
1. With default settings (1 slot): Ollama processes requests sequentially. Extra requests simply wait in a FIFO queue. Total throughput never exceeds ~200 tok/s.
  2. With 4 slots: Throughput doubles from 190 tok/s to 385 tok/s. Each individual stream takes 9.4 ms per token instead of 4.9 ms, but the server delivers 2× more total work.
  3. The Saturation Plateau (8 slots): Going from 4 to 8 slots yields only a 4% increase in throughput (385 → 400 tok/s), while TPOT doubles to 16 ms. The GPU compute is now fully saturated. More slots buy concurrency under the SLO, not higher throughput.

docs.title: Experiment 4: Queueing & The p99 Latency Knee
The Concept
docs.text:
When traffic exceeds slot capacity, requests wait in an arrival queue. * Median latency (\(p50\)) often looks healthy even when the system is beginning to fail. * Tail latency (\(p99\)) is where queueing manifests first.

Where is the "knee" in the latency curve?

docs.title: The Experiment
docs.text: Look at results/ollama-np4.json as concurrency passes the 4-slot limit (\(c=1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8\)):

docs.title: Real Measured Numbers (4 Slots Configured)
docs.text: Concurrency (\(c\)) TTFT p50 TTFT p90 TTFT p99 Queue Status \(c=1\) 43 ms 51 ms 59 ms No queue \(c=2\) 56 ms 88 ms 110 ms No queue \(c=4\) 101 ms 161 ms 197 ms At capacity (all 4 slots busy) \(c=5\) 367 ms 820 ms 943 ms Knee exceeded! Requests wait for slots \(c=6\) 682 ms 1,180 ms 1,410 ms Severe queueing \(c=8\) 1,240 ms 1,480 ms 1,530 ms Queueing delay dominates runtime

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
• Between \(c=4\) and \(c=5\), TTFT p99 jumps by nearly 5× (197 ms → 943 ms)!
  • If you only monitor average or p50 latency, \(c=5\) looks "acceptable" (367 ms), but 10% of your users are waiting almost a full second just to see the first word.
  • This transition point is the knee of the queueing curve.

docs.title: The Concept
docs.text:
In operations research and systems performance, Little's Law states that for any stable queueing system:

\[L = \lambda \times W\]

Where: * \(L\) = Average number of concurrent requests in the system (in-flight). * \(\lambda\) = Average arrival rate / completed throughput (requests per second). * \(W\) = Average time a request spends in the system (End-to-End latency in seconds).

Does this mathematical law hold true in real inference measurements?

docs.title: The Proof
docs.text:
Take the measured data from results/ollama-np4.json at concurrency level \(c=4\): * Completed request throughput \(\lambda = 3.16\text{ req/s}\) * Average E2E latency \(W = 1.27\text{ seconds}\)

Apply Little's Law: $\(L = \lambda \times W = 3.16\text{ req/s} \times 1.27\text{ s} = 4.013\text{ requests}\)$

The calculated in-flight requests (\(4.01\)) matches our closed-loop concurrency setting of \(c=4\) with \(99.7\%\) accuracy.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text: If you know your target E2E latency SLO (\(W\)) and your expected user traffic (\(\lambda\)), Little's Law tells you exactly how many active serving slots (\(L\)) you must provision in GPU VRAM.

docs.title: Experiment 6: Closed Loop vs. Open Loop (Poisson Traffic)
The Concept
docs.text: There are two distinct ways to load-test an inference server: 1. Closed Loop (Concurrency Sweep): The benchmark client maintains \(N\) workers. A worker waits for response \(k\) to finish before sending request \(k+1\). * Problem: If the server slows down, the client automatically slows down. It creates artificial backpressure that hides server collapses. 2. Open Loop (Poisson Arrival Rate): Requests arrive at random, independent intervals according to a Poisson process (\(\lambda\text{ req/s}\)), mimicking real humans clicking "Submit". * If the server slows down, new requests keep arriving anyway. When \(\lambda \ge \mu\) (arrival rate exceeds service rate), queue length diverges to infinity.

docs.title: The Experiment
docs.text:
Compare a closed-loop sweep against an open-loop Poisson rate test (results/learn/rate.json):

# Open-loop Poisson arrivals at 2, 4, 6 requests per second
servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 --model qwen2.5:0.5b \
    --mode rate --levels 1,2,3,4 --input-len 256 --output-len 128 --out results/learn/rate.json

docs.title: Real Measured Numbers
docs.text:
• At \(\lambda = 1.0\text{ req/s}\): Service capacity (\(\mu \approx 3.2\text{ req/s}\)) easily handles traffic. TTFT p50 = 55 ms.
  • At \(\lambda = 2.0\text{ req/s}\): System is healthy; occasional burst causes temporary queueing. TTFT p50 = 68 ms.
  • At \(\lambda \to 3.5\text{ req/s}\): Traffic exceeds maximum service rate. Every subsequent request queues behind accumulated backlog; TTFT and E2E skyrocket until requests time out.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text: Closed-loop tests are great for finding maximum throughput capacity. Open-loop tests are required to find your production breaking point.

docs.title: Experiment 7: Benchmarking Pitfalls
docs.text: When measuring LLM serving systems, three subtle pitfalls produce misleading numbers:

docs.title: Pitfall 1: Prompt Cache Hits (The Seed Trap)
docs.text: Many modern inference engines (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp) cache the KV states of common prompt prefixes. * If you benchmark using the exact same prompt repeatedly without varying the seed, the server reuses the cached KV state from request #1. * In results/learn/cache-seed7.json, reusing the prompt dropped TTFT from 42.2 ms down to 20.4 ms (a 51% artificial latency reduction!). * How servebench handles this: servebench generates fresh random prompt seeds per run by default.

docs.title: Pitfall 2: TCP Connection Overhead on Windows
docs.text:
• On Windows, connecting to localhost attempts an IPv6 (::1) connection before falling back to IPv4 (127.0.0.1), adding up to 270 ms of connection setup latency to every request.
  • Breaking connection pooling between requests causes TTFT to appear artificially inflated.
  • How servebench handles this: Always benchmark against http://127.0.0.1:..., and verify that client connection reuse is maintained across streams.

docs.title: Pitfall 3: Warm-up Bias
docs.text:
• The first 1–2 requests to an LLM endpoint trigger CUDA context initialization, memory allocation, and graph compilation.
  • If included in benchmark summaries, these initial outliers corrupt p99 metrics.
  • How servebench handles this: Always run --warmup 2 unmeasured requests before timing begins.

docs.title: Glossary of Inference Terms
docs.text:
• Prefill: The initial compute phase where the LLM processes all input prompt tokens in parallel and builds the initial KV cache.
  • Decode: The autoregressive generation phase where the LLM produces output tokens one by one, reading the entire model weights and KV cache at each step.
  • TTFT (Time to First Token): Duration from sending the HTTP request until the client receives the first streamed content token. Measures prefill + queueing + network.
  • TPOT (Time Per Output Token): Average duration between generated tokens during the decode phase: \((E2E - TTFT) / (tokens - 1)\).
  • ITL (Inter-Token Latency): The individual time gaps between consecutive streamed chunks.
  • Throughput: Total tokens (or requests) processed per second across all concurrent streams.
  • Goodput: Throughput of requests that strictly meet defined Service Level Objectives (SLOs) (e.g. TTFT < 500 ms and TPOT < 50 ms).
  • KV Cache: The saved Key and Value tensor representations of past tokens in GPU memory, avoiding redundant re-computation of attention.
  • PagedAttention: Allocating KV cache memory in non-contiguous virtual pages (like OS virtual memory) to eliminate memory fragmentation.
  • Continuous Batching (Iteration-level Scheduling): Dynamically inserting new requests into running decode batches at each token step rather than waiting for an entire batch to finish.
  • Little's Law: Fundamental queueing relation \(L = \lambda W\) linking concurrency (\(L\)), throughput (\(\lambda\)), and latency (\(W\)).

docs.title: Metrics Glossary & Mathematical Formulations
docs.text: This document provides rigorous mathematical definitions, explanations, and industry significance for all metrics measured by Servebench.

docs.title: Time to First Token (TTFT)
docs.text:
The duration from the moment the client dispatches the HTTP request to the moment the first non-empty content chunk is parsed.

\[\text{TTFT} = t_{\text{first\_content\_chunk}} - t_{\text{send}}\]
  • Units: seconds / milliseconds.
  • Components: Client network transit + Server queue wait + Engine prompt prefill compute.
  • Significance: Determines the perceived responsiveness of interactive chat applications.

docs.title: Time Per Output Token (TPOT)
docs.text:
The average duration required to generate each token after the first token arrives.

\[\text{TPOT} = \frac{\text{E2E Latency} - \text{TTFT}}{\text{Output Tokens} - 1}\]
  • Units: milliseconds / seconds per token.
  • Significance: Determines reading speed. Human reading speed is approximately \(20-30\text{ ms/token}\) (\(30-50\text{ tokens/s}\)).

docs.title: Inter-Token Latency (ITL)
docs.text:
The sequence of elapsed durations between consecutive content chunks arriving over the streaming Server-Sent Events (SSE) connection:

\[\text{ITL}_i = t_{i} - t_{i-1}\]
  • Significance: While TPOT measures overall generation speed, ITL percentiles (p50, p90, p99) measure smooth token pacing and detect generation stuttering.

docs.title: 2. Server-Side Timing Breakdown (P11)
docs.text:
When using engines like llama.cpp or Ollama that report internal phase durations, Servebench breaks TTFT into: 1. Server Prefill: Time the GPU spent evaluating input prompt tokens. 2. Server Decode: Time the GPU spent generating output tokens. 3. Queue & Network Overhead: $\(\text{Queue/Network Overhead} = \text{Client TTFT} - \text{Server Prefill}\)$

  • Significance: If client TTFT is 200 ms and Server Prefill is only 25 ms, requests are spending 175 ms waiting in line for an available KV cache slot.

docs.title: Output Token Throughput
docs.text:
\[\text{Output Throughput} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \text{Output Tokens}_i}{\text{Wall Duration}}\]
  • Units: tokens per second (tok/s).

docs.title: Steady-State Throughput
docs.text: Throughput calculated over a stable time window that excludes the initial connection warm-up ramp-up and late draining tail.

docs.title: Goodput
docs.text:
The rate of completed tokens delivered by requests that satisfied both target latency Service Level Objectives (SLOs):

\[\text{Goodput} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \text{In-SLO}} \text{Output Tokens}_i}{\text{Wall Duration}}\]

where request \(i\) is in-SLO if: $\(\text{TTFT}_i \le \text{SLO}_{\text{TTFT}} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{TPOT}_i \le \text{SLO}_{\text{TPOT}}\)$

docs.title: Tokens per Joule (Efficiency)
docs.text:
\[\text{Tokens per Joule} = \frac{\text{Output Throughput (tok/s)}}{\text{Average GPU Power (W)}} = \frac{\text{Total Output Tokens}}{\text{Total Energy Consumed (Joules)}}\]
  • Units: tokens per Joule.
  • Significance: Crucial for comparing models across quantization levels (e.g. FP16 vs INT4) and assessing datacenter operational costs.

docs.title: Order Statistics & Percentiles
docs.text:
For any timing distribution, percentiles (p50, p90, p99) are computed via nearest-rank interpolation.

Statistical Warning: When sample size \(N < 100\), computing p99 is mathematically bounded by the sample maximum. Servebench reports sample count \(N\) alongside all percentiles and issues a warning if \(N < 100\).

docs.title: Multi-Trial Repeat Confidence Intervals
docs.text:
When --repeat N is specified, each load level is executed across \(N\) independent runs with fresh seeds. Servebench computes sample mean \(\bar{x}\), sample standard deviation \(s\), and two-tailed Student's t 95% confidence intervals:

\[\text{CI}_{95\%} = \bar{x} \pm t_{0.025, N-1} \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{N}}\]

docs.title: Operational / Arithmetic Intensity (\(I\))
docs.text:
The ratio of floating point operations performed per byte of memory transferred from DRAM/HBM:

\[I = \frac{\text{Floating Point Operations (FLOP)}}{\text{DRAM Memory Transferred (Bytes)}} \quad [\text{FLOP/Byte}]\]
  • Decode Phase: Each autoregressively generated token accesses all model weights once (\(2P\) FLOPs per parameter, reading \(P \times \text{Bytes/Param}\)). At batch size \(c=1\), intensity is \(\approx 1.0\text{ FLOP/Byte}\) (FP16) or \(\approx 4.0\text{ FLOP/Byte}\) (INT4).
  • Batching Amortization: As batch size \(c\) increases, weights are reused across \(c\) tokens, scaling arithmetic intensity \(I \approx c \times I_1\).

docs.title: Ridge Point (\(I_{\text{ridge}}\))
docs.text:
The critical arithmetic intensity where hardware performance transitions from being memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound:

\[I_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{\text{Peak Compute Ceiling (FLOP/s)}}{\text{Peak Memory Bandwidth (Bytes/s)}} \quad [\text{FLOP/Byte}]\]
  • If operational intensity \(I < I_{\text{ridge}}\), the workload is Memory-Bandwidth Bound.
  • If operational intensity \(I \ge I_{\text{ridge}}\), the workload is Compute Bound.

docs.title: Memory Bandwidth Utilization (MBU %)
docs.text:
The fraction of theoretical memory bus throughput achieved by weight streaming during decode:

\[\text{MBU} = \frac{\text{Achieved Memory Bandwidth}}{\text{Peak Hardware Memory Bandwidth}} \times 100\%\]

where: $\(\text{Achieved Memory Bandwidth (GB/s)} = \frac{\text{Decode Tokens/s}}{c} \times \text{Model Size (GB)}\)$

docs.title: Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU %)
docs.text:
The fraction of theoretical peak matrix tensor compute utilized by GEMM operations:

\[\text{MFU} = \frac{\text{Achieved TFLOPs}}{\text{Peak Hardware TFLOPs}} \times 100\%\]

where achieved decode TFLOPs is: $\(\text{Achieved TFLOPs} = \frac{\text{Tokens/s} \times 2 \times \text{Param Count}}{10^{12}}\)$

docs.title: Python API Reference
docs.text: Servebench provides a clean, fully typed Python API for running benchmarks and evaluating performance regressions directly in your scripts, Jupyter notebooks, or custom evaluation harnesses.

docs.title: 1. Top-Level Imports
docs.text:
import servebench
from servebench import (
    benchmark,
    check_regression,
    compare,
    CheckThresholds,
    CheckReport,
    RunResult,
    LevelResult,
    RequestResult,
    Summary,
    Stats,
)

docs.title: 2. Running a Benchmark (servebench.benchmark)
docs.text:
Executes a synchronous benchmark run and returns a RunResult object containing all level summaries, per-request timings, GPU telemetry, and automated bottleneck diagnoses.

import servebench

res = servebench.benchmark(
    url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1",
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3-8B-Instruct",
    mode="concurrency",
    levels=[1, 2, 4, 8],
    num_requests=25,
    preset="chat",             # sets input_len=128, output_len=256
    burstiness=0.8,            # clustered arrivals
    gpu_telemetry=True,        # collect NVML GPU metrics
    scrape_metrics="auto",     # scrape server /metrics
    save_path="results.json",
)

# Inspect peak throughput
peak = max(lv.summary.output_throughput for lv in res.levels)
print(f"Peak Output Throughput: {peak:.1f} tok/s")

# Inspect primary bottleneck
if res.bottleneck_diagnosis:
    print(f"Primary Bottleneck: {res.bottleneck_diagnosis['primary_bottleneck']}")

docs.title: Signature & Parameters
docs.text:
def benchmark(
    url: str,
    model: str,
    *,
    mode: Literal["concurrency", "rate"] = "concurrency",
    levels: list[float] | None = None,
    num_requests: int | None = 20,
    duration: float | None = None,
    input_len: int = 256,
    output_len: int = 128,
    preset: str | None = None,
    burstiness: float = 1.0,
    trace: str | Path | None = None,
    shared_prefix_tokens: int | None = None,
    gpu_telemetry: bool = True,
    scrape_metrics: str | None = None,
    endpoint: Literal["chat", "completions"] = "chat",
    slo_ttft_ms: float | None = 500.0,
    slo_tpot_ms: float | None = 50.0,
    warmup: int = 2,
    seed: int = 0,
    timeout: float = 300.0,
    api_key: str | None = None,
    label: str | None = None,
    save_path: str | Path | None = None,
) -> RunResult:

docs.title: 3. Evaluating Regressions (servebench.check_regression)
docs.text:
Compares a candidate run against a baseline run and verifies whether metrics stayed within tolerances. Accepts RunResult instances or paths to JSON files.

import servebench

# Compare two runs
report = servebench.check_regression(
    candidate="candidate_run.json",
    baseline="baseline_run.json",
    thresholds=servebench.CheckThresholds(
        max_ttft_pct=15.0,
        max_tpot_pct=10.0,
        max_throughput_pct=10.0,
        max_error_rate_pct=1.0,
    )
)

if not report.passed:
    print("Performance regression detected!")
    for failure in report.failures:
        print(f" - {failure}")

docs.title: 4. Multi-Run Comparison (servebench.compare)
docs.text:
Loads and normalizes multiple benchmark runs for comparison.

import servebench

runs = servebench.compare(["run1.json", "run2.json"])
for r in runs:
    peak_tok_s = max(lv.summary.output_throughput for lv in r.levels)
    print(f"{r.label}: {peak_tok_s:.1f} tok/s")

docs.title: 5. Hardware Roofline Analysis (servebench.compute_roofline)
docs.text:
Programmatically compute operational intensity, MBU %, and MFU % across concurrency sweeps:

import servebench

# Load benchmark run
run = servebench.compare(["results/ollama-np4.json"])[0]

# Compute Roofline metrics for RTX 3050 Laptop GPU
analysis = servebench.compute_roofline(
    model_name=run.config.model,
    levels_data=[
        {"concurrency": int(lv.value), "output_tokens_per_s": lv.summary.output_throughput}
        for lv in run.levels
    ],
    gpu_name="RTX 3050 Laptop",
)

print(f"Peak MBU: {analysis.peak_mbu}% | Peak MFU: {analysis.peak_mfu}%")
print(f"Regime: {analysis.primary_regime}")

# Print ASCII roofline curve
print(servebench.render_ascii_roofline(analysis))

docs.title: 6. Auto-Tuning Engine (servebench.evaluate_tuning)
docs.text:
Analyze concurrency sweeps, determine saturation knees, and generate tailored launch configurations:

import servebench

run = servebench.compare(["results/ollama-np4.json"])[0]

report = servebench.evaluate_tuning(
    run=run,
    engine_override="ollama",
    target_ttft_p50_ms=150.0,
    target_itl_p50_ms=40.0,
)

rec = report.recommendation
print(f"Optimal concurrency: {rec.recommended_concurrency}")
print(f"Launch command: {rec.launch_command_example}")
